# What this document is

This is Lecture 11 as a written tutorial, in the same order as the script
`lecture11_models.R`. It follows *Business Analytics* (Camm et al.), Chapters 8.4 and 8.5,
10.2 and 10.3, and 11.1 to 11.4, and Chapter 5 of *Tidyverse Skills for Data Science*
(Wright et al.). Open the `.Rmd` file in RStudio and press **Knit** to rebuild this PDF.

In Lecture 10 you fitted a straight line with one $x$: $y = \alpha + \beta x + \varepsilon$.
Today you use several $x$ variables, then predict a $y$ that is only yes or no, and then
predict from the most similar cases with k-nearest neighbours, checked on data the model
has not seen.

# Packages and the data

`install.packages()` is needed once per computer; `library()` every session. Two packages
are new today: `car` gives `vif()`, and `class` gives `knn()` (it comes with R).

```{r install, eval=FALSE}
install.packages("tidyverse")        # once per computer. Installed in Lecture 3
install.packages("broom")            # once per computer. Installed in Lecture 10
install.packages("GGally")           # once per computer. Installed in Lecture 7
install.packages("car")              # once per computer. New today
install.packages("class")            # once per computer. New today
```

```{r packages}
library(tidyverse)                   # loads ggplot2, dplyr and the rest
library(broom)                       # loads tidy() and glance()
library(GGally)                      # loads ggpairs()
library(car)                         # loads vif()
library(class)                       # loads knn()
```

The data are 20 patients with high blood pressure, saved as `data/bloodpress.csv` in the
lecture folder.

```{r data}
bp <- read_csv("data/bloodpress.csv")  # 20 patients with high blood pressure
glimpse(bp)                          # 20 rows, 7 columns, all numbers
```

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `BP` | blood pressure in mm Hg: the $y$ |
| `Age` | years |
| `Weight` | kg |
| `BSA` | body surface area, square metres |
| `Dur` | years since the diagnosis |
| `Pulse` | beats per minute |
| `Stress` | a stress score from a questionnaire |

# Multiple linear regression

**Multiple linear regression** explains one dependent variable $y$ by two or more
independent variables:

$$y = \alpha + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \dots + \beta_k x_k + \varepsilon$$

Each $\beta$ is the change in $y$ when its $x$ goes up by 1, **holding the other $x$
variables constant**. In the formula of `lm()`, `+` means "and".

```{r fit2}
fit2 <- lm(BP ~ Age + Weight, data = bp)  # BP explained by Age and Weight
summary(fit2)                        # the estimates, standard errors, p-values, R-squared
```

The estimated equation is

$$\text{BP} = -16.58 + 0.708 \times \text{Age} + 1.033 \times \text{Weight}$$

- **Age, 0.708**: one year older, same weight: blood pressure about 0.71 mm Hg higher, on average.
- **Weight, 1.033**: one kg heavier, same age: about 1.03 mm Hg higher.
- **Intercept, -16.58**: BP at age 0 and weight 0 kg: far outside the data, no practical meaning.
- **$R^2$ = 0.99**: age and weight together explain 99% of the variation in blood pressure in these 20 patients.

"Holding the other $x$ variables constant" means comparing people who differ in one $x$
only: two patients of 95 kg, aged 50 and 51, differ by 0.71 mm Hg. A prediction needs a
value for every $x$ in the model:

```{r predict2}
# BP for a 50-year-old who weighs 95 kg
predict(fit2, newdata = tibble(Age = 50, Weight = 95))
```

By hand: $-16.58 + 0.708 \times 50 + 1.033 \times 95 = 117.0$.

# Inference and regression

Two kinds of test, with the same decision rule: **p-value below 0.05, reject $H_0$**; the
result is statistically significant. A p-value of 0.05 or above means we cannot reject
$H_0$, which is not proof that the effect is zero.

- **t-test**, one $\beta$ at a time. $H_0$: $\beta = 0$, this $x$ does not help, given the others.
- **F-test**, the whole model. $H_0$: all $\beta$ are 0, no $x$ helps at all.

```{r fit6}
# all six x variables
fit6 <- lm(BP ~ Age + Weight + BSA + Dur + Pulse + Stress, data = bp)
summary(fit6)                        # Age, Weight, BSA significant; Dur, Pulse, Stress not
```

Age, Weight and BSA are significant. Dur, Pulse and Stress are not: once age, weight and
BSA are in the model, they add no clear information. The last line is the F-test: F =
560.6, p = 6.4e-15, so at least one $x$ is related to blood pressure. The tests rely on the
four conditions of Lecture 10 for the error term and on no strong multicollinearity.

`tidy()` gives the same coefficient table as a tibble, and `glance()` the model numbers:

```{r tidy6}
tidy(fit6)                           # the same coefficient table as a tibble
glance(fit2)                         # R-squared 0.9914, adjusted 0.9904
glance(fit6)                         # R-squared 0.9962, adjusted 0.9944
```

$R^2$ is the share of the variation in $y$ that the model explains. It **never goes down**
when we add an $x$, even a useless one. **Adjusted $R^2$** subtracts a penalty for every
extra $x$, so use it to compare models with a different number of $x$ variables.

# Multicollinearity

**Multicollinearity**: two or more $x$ variables are strongly correlated with each other.
Heavier people have a larger body surface, so Weight and BSA carry almost the same
information. The model cannot tell which of the two is responsible: the standard errors
grow, and the estimates change a lot when a variable is added or removed. The predictions of
the model as a whole are not harmed.

Two ways to detect it: the correlation matrix of the $x$ variables ($|r|$ above 0.8 is a
warning), and the variance inflation factor.

```{r ggpairs, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5.2}
bp |>
  select(Age, Weight, BSA, Dur, Pulse, Stress) |>  # the six x variables
  ggpairs()                          # scatter plots below, correlations above
```

```{r cor}
bp |>
  select(Age, Weight, BSA, Dur, Pulse, Stress) |>  # the six x variables
  cor() |>                           # the correlation matrix
  round(2)                           # two decimals. Weight and BSA: 0.88
```

The **variance inflation factor (VIF)**, one per $x$: 1 means no correlation with the
others, above 5 is a worry, above 10 is serious.

```{r vif6}
vif(fit6)                            # variance inflation factor, one per x
```

Weight (8.4) and BSA (5.3) are above 5. Removing one of the pair is the simplest remedy:

```{r fit5}
# the same model without BSA
fit5 <- lm(BP ~ Age + Weight + Dur + Pulse + Stress, data = bp)
vif(fit5)                            # all VIFs now below 5
glance(fit5)                         # adjusted R-squared 0.992: almost nothing lost
```

Other remedies: combine the two into one index when that makes sense, or use
regularisation, such as ridge regression, which keeps all variables but shrinks their
estimates. Multicollinearity is a problem for interpreting the estimates, not for
predicting.

# Logistic regression

When $y$ has two values, coded 1 (yes) and 0 (no), a straight line predicts values below 0
and above 1, which cannot be probabilities. **Logistic regression** predicts the
**probability** that $y = 1$, always between 0 and 1, on an S-shaped curve.

The data are `mtcars`, 32 cars that come with R. `am` is 1 for a manual gearbox and 0 for
an automatic; `wt` is the weight in 1000 lbs.

```{r logit}
glimpse(mtcars)                      # 32 cars, 11 columns
# glm() with family = binomial is logistic regression
logit <- glm(am ~ wt, data = mtcars, family = binomial)
summary(logit)                       # wt: -4.02, p = 0.005
```

Read the sign: $-4.02$, so heavier cars are **less likely** to be manual. The p-value,
0.005, is below 0.05: weight is significant. The size of the estimate is on the log-odds
scale, which is hard to read, so we use predicted probabilities instead.

```{r curve, echo = FALSE}
curve <- tibble(wt = seq(1.4, 5.5, by = 0.02)) |>
  mutate(prob = predict(logit, newdata = tibble(wt = wt), type = "response"))
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, y = am)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line(data = curve, aes(x = wt, y = prob)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Weight (1000 lbs)", y = "am: 1 = manual, 0 = automatic")
```

`type = "response"` gives the probability. With a **cut-off of 0.5**, a probability above
0.5 predicts 1 (manual), otherwise 0. `if_else(test, value if TRUE, value if FALSE)` does
this row by row.

```{r classes}
cars <- mtcars |>
  mutate(prob = predict(logit, type = "response"),  # type = "response" gives probabilities
         pred = if_else(prob > 0.5, 1, 0))          # cut-off 0.5: above it, predict manual

cars |>
  select(wt, am, prob, pred) |>      # the columns we need
  head()                             # first six cars

# a car of 3000 lbs: probability 0.49
predict(logit, newdata = tibble(wt = 3), type = "response")
```

The **confusion matrix** counts the actual classes against the predicted ones: true
positives and true negatives are correct; a false positive is a false alarm, a false
negative a missed yes. **Accuracy** is the share of correct predictions.

```{r confusion}
cars |>
  count(am, pred)                    # the confusion matrix: actual am against predicted
cars |>
  summarise(accuracy = mean(am == pred))  # share predicted correctly: 0.91 (29 of 32)
```

These are the same 32 cars the model learned from. A fair check uses new data.

# k-nearest neighbours, and train and test

**k-nearest neighbours (kNN)** predicts a new case from the $k$ most similar cases we
already know. The idea: similar things are close together. kNN fits no line; it keeps the
data and compares. The four steps:

1. **Choose $k$**, the number of neighbours.
2. **Measure the distance** from the new point to every known point. The Euclidean
   distance is the straight-line distance, as with a ruler:
   $d = \sqrt{(x_1 - x_1')^2 + (x_2 - x_2')^2}$.
3. **Take the $k$ closest.**
4. **Vote**: for classification, the new point gets the most common class among them; for
   regression, the average of their values.

## Example: which T-shirt size for a new customer?

We know the height, weight and T-shirt size of 18 customers. A new customer is 162 cm and
58 kg. We compute the distance from the new customer to every known customer and keep the
five closest ($k = 5$).

```{r shirts}
shirts <- tibble(
  height = c(158, 158, 158, 160, 160, 163, 163, 160, 163,
             165, 165, 165, 168, 168, 168, 170, 170, 170),  # height in cm
  weight = c(58, 59, 63, 59, 60, 60, 61, 64, 64,
             61, 62, 65, 62, 63, 66, 63, 64, 68),            # weight in kg
  size   = c("M", "M", "M", "M", "M", "M", "M", "L", "L",
             "L", "L", "L", "L", "L", "L", "L", "L", "L"))   # T-shirt size

shirts |>
  mutate(distance = sqrt((height - 162)^2 +
                         (weight - 58)^2)) |>  # distance to the new customer
  arrange(distance) |>               # closest first
  slice_head(n = 5)                  # the 5 nearest (k = 5)
```

All five nearest customers wear M, so we predict size **M** for the new customer.

## Example: kNN for a number

| Experience (years) | Income (1000 dollars) | Distance to 5 years |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 25 | 4 |
| 2 | 28 | 3 |
| **4** | **45** | **1** |
| **6** | **60** | **1** |
| **7** | **65** | **2** |

For a new person with 5 years of experience and $k = 3$, the three nearest are 4, 6 and 7
years. The prediction is the average of their incomes: $(45 + 60 + 65) / 3 = 56.7$, so
56,700 dollars.

## Train and test

The model learns from the **training set**, usually 80% of the rows chosen at random, like
studying past exam questions. It then predicts the **test set**, the other 20%, like a new
exam, and we compare with the true values. On the data it learned from, a model can look
perfect because it has memorised them; only new data show whether it generalises.

The data for the R example are `iris`, 150 flowers of three species that come with R.

```{r split}
flowers <- iris |>
  mutate(id = row_number())          # a number for every flower, to split by

set.seed(2026)                       # makes the random split the same every time
train <- flowers |>
  slice_sample(prop = 0.8)           # a random 80%: 120 flowers
test <- flowers |>
  anti_join(train, by = "id")        # the other 20%: 30 flowers
```

```{r iris-plot}
ggplot(train, aes(x = Petal.Length, y = Petal.Width, colour = Species)) +
  geom_point() +                     # the training flowers
  labs(x = "Petal length (cm)", y = "Petal width (cm)")
```

`knn()` takes the $x$ columns of the training and test rows, the true classes of the
training rows (`cl`), and $k$.

```{r knn}
train_x <- train |>
  select(Petal.Length, Petal.Width)  # the x variables of the training flowers
test_x <- test |>
  select(Petal.Length, Petal.Width)  # the x variables of the test flowers

set.seed(2026)                       # knn() breaks ties at random
# k = 5 neighbours
pred5 <- knn(train = train_x, test = test_x, cl = train$Species, k = 5)

test <- test |>
  mutate(pred = pred5)               # add the predicted species to the test table
test |>
  count(Species, pred)               # the confusion matrix
test |>
  summarise(accuracy = mean(Species == pred))  # share of test flowers classified correctly
```

29 of the 30 test flowers are classified correctly: accuracy 0.97 on flowers the method
had not seen. The one error is a versicolor taken for a virginica.

**Choosing $k$.** A small $k$ follows every single point, including noise: overfitting. A
large $k$ smooths too much: underfitting. Try several values and keep the one with the best
test accuracy; an odd $k$ avoids ties between two classes. **Units matter**: kNN works with
distances, so put the $x$ variables on the same scale first when they are in different
units. Petal length and width are both in cm.

# The three methods side by side

| | Multiple linear regression | Logistic regression | k-nearest neighbours |
|---|---|---|---|
| $y$ is | a number | yes or no (1 or 0) | a class or a number |
| It gives | a predicted number | a probability, then a class | the majority class or the average |
| In R | `lm()` | `glm(family = binomial)` | `knn()` |
| We read | $\beta$s, p-values, adjusted $R^2$ | signs, p-values, probabilities | accuracy on the test set |
